allen-chapman-haywood-district-1881-06-0.A1:
Murder by Georgia Regulators.
Columbus, Ga., June 7.—For some time considerable excitement has been caused in Haywood district, Chattooga county, from the fact that Allen Chapmen, a colored man, wss living and co-habiting with a very comely girl of pure white blood.

Warnings had been sent to both of them in an anonymous way several times, that if they continued to inhabit the same cabin there would be trouble.

These warnings were not heeded, and ominous mutterings of a disturbance began to fill the air. Last night a band of men, masked and armed, made their appearance at his door and demanded the girl. In her place Chapman, the colored man, presented himself with a shot gun, The crowd at once opened fire upon him. flicking his body full of shot and retreated. Chapman was horribly wounded, and is now reported dead.

archie-walker-waco-1881-09.A1:
TELEGRAPHIC JOTTINGS.
Ross having replied to Hanlan's telegram, declining to row for more than $1,000, the latter has signed articles to row for $1,000 on the 15th of November, the course to be mutually agreed upon. The articles were sent to Ross for his signature. Ross will accept Hanlan's proposition to row on November 15. The race will probably be at Silver Lake, Mass.

The citizens of Waco, Miss., took Archie Walker, a negro, who attempted to outrage the daughter of Capt. Lee, and hanged him to a tree.

Hon. Lionel Sackville West, the English minister, has postponed his departure for Washington until the middle of October.

Mr. Lowell, American minister at London, is about to take a month's holiday, which he will spend in Scotland.

Frank Williams, alias Elo, just released from Auburn penitentiary was sent from Washington last night on a requisition from Boston, where is wanted for the robbery of some jewelry.

Base ball yesterday: At Boston, Bostons 3, Cleveland 4; at Worcester, Chicago 4, Worcesters 12; at Providence, Buffalos 9, Providence 3; at Troy, Detroitis 4, Troys 3.

NOTES FROM OUR NEIGHBORS.
Carlisle, Arkansas, boasts of a new and handsome school building.

There are a great many projectors from the north in central Arkansas.

Since August 31st, last, forty-seven gin-houses have been burned in Alabama.

In the district court that closed at Corsicana, Texas, last week there were nine felony convictions.

A new saw and shingle mill has been erected on Cache river, about two miles east of Surrounded Hill, Arkansas.

The Houston Post "is fast coming to the conclusion that the constitution of Texas was a poorly patched up job in 1875."

John L. Martin, an escaped convict, was captured at Laredo, Texas, a few days ago. He has seventeen years to serve.

The Gadsden, Alabama, foundry is doing a good business. They cast a great deal of hollowware, which find a ready market.

Wesson, Mississippi, is a very thriving town, and its population orderly and temperate. There is not a grogshop in the town.

The cotton factory at Tuscaloosa, Alabama, turns out about 25,000 yards of nice, smooth goods per week, at a handsome net profit.

The Agricultural and Mechanical college of Mississippi, under the direction of General Stephen D. Lee, has so far been a gratifying success.

A dispatch from McKinney, Texas, on the 23d of February, states that Ex-Governor Throckmorton was taken sick with symptoms of meningitis.

Mr. Peter Fresenius, civil engineer, who had been connected with railroads in the south for a long while, died at his residence in Mobile last Friday.

George Hall, of Nashville, wanted John Ryan to credit him for drinks. Ryan refused. Hall went out, secured a shotgun, and without a word shot Ryan in the head.

The Nashville American claims to have good authority for saying that Governor Hawkins will not call an extra session of the legislature for the settlement of the State debt.

Among the distinguished gentlemen who have been mentioned in connection with the governorship of Mississippi, we notice the name of Judge Upton M. Young, of Vicksburg.

Joseph Crockett, a negro, charged with murder and arson at Corinth, Mississippi, was arrested at Palestine, Tennessee, on the twenty-third. He is said to be the author of many crimes, and a refugee from Louisiana.

The Aberdeen Examiner is assured by a telegram from Major Gordon, who is in Montgomery, Alabama, that work on the railroad from Aberdeen east will be commenced soon, and that the enterprise is considered a "fix fact."

On Sunday last the dwelling house of Mrs. Mary Varnum, Etowah county, Alabama, was consumed by fire, together with the greater portion of the household goods. The fire was accidental, supposed to have caught from a spark from the chimney.

Last week a negro ravished a white lady at Refugio, Texas, whose name is withheld. After the act she followed him a mile, trying to kill him with an ax, but he escaped. The brute was subsequently captured and jailed. A mob took him out and hung him.

At Austin, Texas, on the 26th of February, Judge Weir was sentenced to the penitentiary for five years for forgery of land titles. He is seventy years old, and has been for thirty-five years a respected citizen of Leon county. A motion was made for a new trial.

There is a bill now on its passage through the senate of Texas for the sale of school lands. It provides that they are to be sold in lots of not less than 160 acres, nor more than one section to one person. The object of this law is to prevent land speculators from monopolizing the lands.

Spinal meningitis is prevailing at Dallas, Fort Worth, Weatherford and other towns in north Texas. The Denison News, of the twenty-second, says: "There is no longer any doubt that the dreadful disease has made its appearance in this city. Four cases are reported by the physicians. It is principally confined to children."

The cotton-seed of the November and December pickings are reported in many localities in north Alabama as worthless. Many of them will germinate and bring a sickly plant which will die with the first dry cool spell in May or June. The Guntersville Denocrat suggests that a careful examination might avert serious trouble.

A tragedy occurred last Sunday morning in Carter county, Tennessee, about a mile and a half from Elizabethtown, in which George Colbaugh was shot by Mrs. Sarah Smith. The scoundrel, because she would not marry him, circulated reports defamatory to her character, and which caused her recently married and cowardly husband to leave her.

On last Tuesday night James O'Connor, who, for several months past, has been in the employ of the Texas and Pacific railway in the capacity of a locomotive fireman, was shot and instantly killed by James Gibbons, the proprietor of a saloon and eating-stand at the freight depot, Marshall, Texas. It was a cold-blooded and deliberate murder.

The much-talked-of feat of eating thirty partridges in as many consecutive days, has been recently performed by Miss Lee, who resides with her brother-in-law, Mr. Josiah H. Smith, of Carlowville, Dallas county, Alabama. Instead of feeling any discomfort on account of it, Miss Lee thinks she could relish and digest a plump partridge every day for any period.

Russell dead, lying on the edge of the hearth in his cabin, south of the river, in the thirteenth district of Knox county, Tennessee. He had his clothes on, and had evidently fallen dead there the night before are he had gone to bed.

The act apportionment representatives to the different counties of Alabama has been published. All the counties remain as they are, except as follows: Cullman, which has heretofore had no representative, will hereafter have one; Lauderdale, heretofore with one member, will have two, and Macon, instead of two, will have one; Mobile will have four instead of five members. The total number is 100.

TEXAS TOPICS.
Sixteen Alabamians got off the train at Dodd City the other day.

Lampasas county has had a light frost, but no damage was done to the fruit.

Three prisoners from Lampasas county were carried to the penitentiary last week.

In 1840 Texas produced 20,000 bales of cotton; in 1870, 800,000 bales, and in 1880, 1,000,000.

The county tax of McLennan county is only twelve and one-half cents on the hundred dollars.

The contract has been let for the erection of a number of United States buildings at San Antonio.

Henry Berleth, a citizen of Galveston for thirty-four years, died on the 17th inst., in his eighty-fifth year.

The Texas & Pacific railroad is said to have reduced freight and passenger rates about ten per cent.

Brenham has an extra supply of thieves, and nightly raids are being made on pantries and smokehouses.

The Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe road has determined to locate its shops and round houses at Belton.
Waco has a cotton seed oil mill boom. Memphis capitalists are there to invest money in that business.

On the night of the 12th some unknown person broke into the Anderson jail and liberated all the prisoners.

Almost every county in the state has sent a petition to the legislature urging the passage of the prohibition bill.

Woodhull Brothers, of Kinney county, have shipped fourteen car loads of mutton sheep, 2800 head, to St. Louis.

The number of counties in Texas has increased from 117 in 1871, to 162 in 1880; an increase of 45 in nine years, or five yearly.

All the cotton from around McDade, on the Austin branch of the Houston and Texas Central railroad, has not yet been sent to market.

The British steamship, Alvah, from Cardiff, Wales, arrived at Galveston Saturday, with 7,350 iron rails for the Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad.

In Galveston, for the week ending Friday the 18th inst., there were twelve deaths, the deceased ranging in age from still-born to eighty-four years of age.

Mr. Redpath, the lecturer in the interest of the Irish land leauge, has notified the Irish citizens of San Antonio that he will shortly tecture in that city.

Cressett: Seymour is looking up. When she gets up she will then look down—upon her less fortunate sister towns. Two more lawyers are billed for Seymour.

The remnants of the old East Texas railroad were seized at Beaumont Thursday by a deputy United States marshal at the instance of Kouritge Bros., of New York.

Never in the history of the state has there been anything to equal the number of excursionists, land prospectors and capitalists, who are now swarming over Texas looking for profitable investments for their capital.

A gentleman living at Jasper has obtained a contract to make one hundred thousand barrel staves. This is a new industry in Texas, and will doubtless prove a paying investment.

The body of an unknown man was found hanging by the neck to the limb of a tree, and with nine bullet holes in his body near near Jacksboro a few days ago. He was tolerably dead.

Decatur Tribune: Isn't it about time for somebody to take hold of the Decatur railroad boom, shake it up and see if it still lives? There are various rumors in the air, but nothing has assumed tangible shape yet.

A practical cotton manufacturer, now visiting San Antonio, says that a mill costing $175,000, and consuming four bales of cotton a day, located there, would have an annual advantage over a similar mill in Massachusetts of $30,000.

The editor of the Clarksville Standard wants county courts to have jurisdiction over all criminal offenses below the grade of capital, and that the judges of said courts should be of the grade and qualifications of the judges of the district court.

At Refugio, a negro ravished a white woman, who tried to take the life of the brute with an axe. He escaped from the outraged woman, but was subsequently captured and jailed. Afterward he was taken from jail by force, to meet a deserved and violent death.

Waco Examiner: Rev. J. W. Piner, one of the oldest and most popular methodist ministers of north Texas, died at his home in Honey Grove, on Saturday last. The writer knew Mr. Piner well. He was the true type of the christian gentleman. We extend our sympathy to the bereaved family.

The Cuero Bulletin says the machinery of the Excelsior cotton factory at that place, is being rapidly put in place by experienced hands. There is material enough on hand to work until the coming in of the next crop. A large number of hands will be engaged.

Presidio county is about to take on a boom. Many persons are settling in the county, where there is a magnificent range for stock. Many fine farms are being opened, and the cultivation of sugar cane has been considered one of the things that will pay there. Its mideral deposits have already caused much excitement.

charles-dew-1881-04.A6:
An Outrage.
LANSING, Mich., Aug. 26.—News was received here to-day from Riley township, Clinton county, to the effect that Charley Dew, a colored farmer, was found in his granary dead hanging to a beam, with the left side of his head laid open by a terrible gash, evidently made by an axe. Last spring he was visited by masked men, who treated him to a coat of tar and feathers. A few days ago he went to St. John's, to the county seat, for the purpose of commencing legal proceedings against parties whom he believed were the perpetrators of the outrage. He lived alone.
charles-dew-1881-04.A7:
Tragical Tales.
A dispatch from Brackett, Texas, dated the 26th inst., says: "While four horse thieves, belonging to an extensive gang which have been operating along the Rio Grande for a long time, were being brought to this place yesterday in charge of officers, they were attacked near the town of Dolores, and all the thieves killed."

At Forest City, Ark., on the night of the 27th inst., Lute Wallace invited S. C. Apperson, city marshal, to take a cigar, and while standing at the corner of the saloon Apperson drew a revolver and said: "I think I will shoot you." Wallace, thinking he was jesting, replied, "Shoot away." Apperson was killed for the murder, for the two men were apparently on the murder, the best of terms.

In a street brawl at Silverton, Col., on the 27th., D. G. Ogsbury was killed by roughs.

Charles Dew, a negro, was murdered at his house in Riley township, Clinton county, Mich., on the night of the 23d inst. He was quarrelsome and had abused his wife. Several days ago unknown men men tarred and feathered him.

While James Boyd, of Owensville, Ky., was watching at the bedside of his sick sister, Mrs. McClure, some unknown person person through the window at Boyd. The shock caused Mrs. McClure's death.

A man named Holt was killed at Washington Springs, Chickasaw Nation, on the 26th inst. A dispute over a game of cards.

A gang of desperadoes who had been committing lawless acts in Dangerfield, Titus, Hopkins, Hunt and Trayson, Texas, were pursued by citizens who succeeded in killing one of the outlaws.

Ben Blanton, ex-sheriff of Cook County, had a difficulty with a man named James Todd, who had been a witness against him, and each vowed wengeance on the other. The men met and began shooting at once and both were instantly killed.

John Hermann, a livery stable keeper, and formerly city marshal of Deshler, O., was shot and instantly killed by Peter Cole, a drayman. The killing is the result of a long-standing feud between these two men.

Unknown parties entered the jail at Monroe, La., on the morning of the 23d inst., and secured Perry Mason and Alex. Wilson, (colored) charged with murder, and hanged them.

A tragedy occurred about ten miles from Edgefield County, S. C., on the 24th inst., between J. W. Buzzard and his son and J. W. Timmerman, in which Timmerman was killed and Buzzard and his son seriously injured. An old feud was the cause of the affair. The weapons used were double-barreled shot-guns.

An unknown assassin killed Alderian Pitts, a wealthy and highly respected farmer of Rutherford County, Penn., on the 22d inst. It is thought the cause of the killing originated from a divorce suit instituted some time since between Pitts and his wife.

A teamster named House and Cal Hatcher, a hackman, had a quarrel at Kansas City, Mo., on the 22d inst., about temporary shed room occupied by teams, and House shot Hatcher through the abdomen. House escaped and is still at large. Hatcher will die.

Two desperadoes named Folsom and Hobbs, having lost money in a gambling place at Waldron, Scott county, Texas, returned to the place the following night and shot John Stewart the keeper of the place. Billy Messingale who was visiting the Stewart family received a ball through the head, and will die.

Orange, Texas, is in a ferment, owing to recent lawless acts, and the citizens have thus far hanged six miscreants—Bob and Sam Saxon and four negroes. At last accounts Charles Delno was about to be tried by a "Kangaroo" court of lynchers and the county is being secured by regulators.
charles-dew-1881-04.A10: With regret we observe that the demon of violence still possesses the lawless North, and that in Clinton county, Mich., (Republican of course), a negro farmer has just been brutally lynched. He was, the telegram says, "not of a quarrelsome disposition," hence not long ago the neighbors tarred and feathered him; then, when he proceeded to take legal action, attacked him by night, split his skull open, dislocated his leg and hunged him, "after a desperate struggle." And while this scene of lawlessness and butchery is being enacted at Senator Conger's backdoor, as we might say, the Senator is up in the woods of Manitoba killing buffaloes and blackflies and other game, and laying the foundation for a whole wilderness of fish stories! In his absence, theresfore, it devolves upon us to catch up the fish-horn of indignation and bellow through it our preparedness to have somebody else wade knee deep if necessary, to assert the sublime truth that this is a Nation, and that the harmless colored man shall be protected in life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness wherever the stars and stripes fly. Never will we consent to disband or consider our mission accomplished till this is recognized, and Michigan has been redeemed by main force—by blood and iron, if need be—from the violence and lawlessness which now disgrace her. You hear us?—N. Y. World.

Widely extended and very destructive forest fires are raging in the Saginaw valley, and the greatest alarm is felt. Many farm buildings have been burned, and families left entirely destitute have sought shelter in the villages. Porter's station, on the St. Louis railroad, was destroyed, and Reese, Vassar and Millington and other towns are endangered. The running of trains has been interfered with and telegraph wires are down. The ground is so very dry that no relief is expected until it rains, although the whole population is fighting the fires wherever it is possible.

The body of Ex-alderman Schultz of Detroit was found in the river. He had been missing for several days.

The Swedish church at Muskegon and its contents, valued at $1,500 was entirely destroyed by fire. It was partially insured.

Daniel Everett of Girard township, had his barn and sheds, with all their contents, burned loss about $1,500; insured for $1,000.

The house, barn and contents belonging to Lan West, at Orión, caught from a marsh which was fired by a passing engine and was burned. Loss, $1,200; insurance, $500.

Mrs. Tyrrell, an old resident of Kalamazoo, died at that place aged 92 years.

Burglars broke into the safe of C. S. Crandall's grocery store at Harbor Springs and escaped with about $400.

While a steam-thresher was running on the farm of John Welch of Sunfield, sparks set fire to a straw stack, which burned, together with a barn and contents, and adjoluing buildings. Loss, $1,200; insured in the Continental. The woods near by caught fire, and it was with great difficulty that a general conflagration was prevented.

John Berry, formerly of Brockway Center, St. Clair county, was found dead in the woods near one of Ward's camps, and was brought down to Ludington for interment.

Reed City is to have water works.

The board of officers appointed to select the companies of state troops to go to Yorktown, have designated the following: 1st regiment Co. A., Ann Arbor; Co. B., Adrian; 2nd regiment, Co. B., Grand Rapids; Co. G., Ionia; 3rd regiment, Co. D., Bay City; Co. E., East Saginaw.

The forest fires now raging in the eastern part of the state nearly equal those of 10 years ago, and in some places are reported as even worse. There has been a frightful loss of life, just how large cannot be told. A number of horrible deaths are reported at Richmondville, including those of three persons roasted alive in a well. The total number of deaths thus far reported is about 20, and it seems likely that the end is not yet. A woman in Sanilac county locked her two children in the house to go for help against the approaching fire, and returned to find that the house had burned and her children had perished in it. A great many people are fleeing to the lake shore to save their lives. The fires appear worst in Saginaw, Tuscola and Sanilac counties, but are breaking out at many points. Several villages are burned and many others threatened. The fires sweep over farms so as to kill even the pigs and chickens, and a great many families are left entirely destitute and must be aided at once.

J. R. Wright & Co.'s planing mill at Port Huron has been burned together with a large amount of dressed lumber. Loss $20,000. Insurance $3,000.

John D. Bennett of Palmer Station, was committed at Hastings in default of bail, on a charge of obtaining goods under false pretenses.

Hon. John M. Harris, Judge of the Probate Court, Grand Rapids, is sued for breach of promise by Miss Hattle Holcourt. Damages claimed $10,000.

The new state asylum is to be located with special reference to the requirements of a distinct northern district.

Samuel Massey's saw and shingle mill, located one mile south of McBrides, was burned. Loss $3,000; insurance $2,000.

It is impossible to at present define the extent of the destruction of life and property by the forest fires. Huron and Sanilac counties may be said to be devastated. Reports are contradictory and unsatisfactory, communication being in many instances completely cut off. A great loss of life has certainly occured. Probably 200 is much below the aggregate. The tales of suffering and death are harrowing in the extreme.

The Michigan forest fires prove to be in destruction of life and property the greatest calamity of the year. The lives lost are estimated at 200 at the lowest, and reports indicate that the figure is likely to be considerably higher. The great disaster was confined almost exclusively to Sanilac and Huron counties. One man traveling about the burnt district is said to have seen the bodies of 116 persons killed by the fire. Forty-five bodies have been found in a single village. The towns back from the shore in Sanilac and Huron counties, from which little has before been heard, are found to have suffered terribly, although no detailed reports are yet given. Through great districts the destruction is complete, and the fire is ended. The sufferings among those who escaped with their lives is severe and widespread, and urgent calls for aid are heard upon every hand. Hundreds and thousands of people, many of these but yesterday well-to-do, are flecking into villages entirely destitute and fairly naked and hungry. In the Saginaw Valley the fires are subsiding, and in some localities rains have ended all danger.

Hulbert Hall of Clio is held for an assault with intent to kill John Z. Richards whom he dangerously injured.

F. D. Lacey's shingle mill at Nirvana was entirely destroyed by fire. Loss $2,500; no insurance.

As later reports come in the worst fears in regard to the Michigan fires are realized. A great tract in Sanilac and Huron counties, 100 miles long on the shore and 20 to 60 miles deep, is mostly burned over, involving a loss of life estimated at from 300 to 1,000, and of property to the extent of millions. Many of the details are almost too horrible for belief. The call for help grows more and more urgent, and already a great many thousand dollars are subscribed, and the whole country is becoming aroused to the work.

The body of Thos. Green, who disappeared from Coldwater, about three months since, has been found hanging to a tree in the outskirts of that city.

Rev. Reed Stuart, pastor of the Battle Creek Presbyterian Church, is not quite stiff enough in his orthodoxy to suit some of the veteran saints who have sat under his ministrations, and therefore the brethren and sisters gathered together recently and talked the thing over with him. The clerk of the church wrote down some of the things said, and sent the record to the presbytery, where Mr. Stuart was confronted by them in the shape of a charge of heresy. He came home, and, in the language of the world's people, "made a kick about it," and the record was wiped off the recording books. The question of indorsing the pastor was then tested by a resolution declaring that the church committee was of the opinion that his pulpit ministrations were sound and in accordance with the teachings of the good book, but the resolution was tabled. Mr. Stuart then resigned, but the church society has since voted to retain him, and ask him to withdraw his resignation.

St. John, Clinton county, has had an exciting murder trial, lasting two weeks and resulting in a verdict of acquittal. Chesley Dew (colored), the murdered man, had lived for many years in the southern part of Clinton county, and by his coarseness and cruelty to his stock had made himself universally detested by his neighbors, some of whom, a short time previous to his murder, had administered a heavy coat of tar and feathers. This was some time last August, and a few weeks subsequently he was found hanging in his barn, bound hand and foot, his skull broken and with other evidence of rough usage. Suspicion pointed to one Ben Cooper, another colored man, living on the Dew farm, and to Dew's wife, Cooper's sister. Their trial was delayed from time to time until the term just closed. The evidence produced was all circumstantial and, it seems, was not strong enough to warrant a conviction. The case was conducted with singular zeal and ability on both sides.

The Albion Mirror relates the following bird-story: Some four years ago we built a little birdhouse, fastened it on top of a pole and raised it in our dooryard. The first year the little blue birds took possession of it, and were apparently very happy in their new home. After about ten days a couple of martins were seen flying about and lighting upon the little blue birds' home, just as though they had a warranty deed for that and all similar effects. The blue birds resented the intrusion and trespass and fought the martins away bravely and successfully. The martins, however, before they finally retired from the contest, called their brother and sister martins to their assistance, to the number of ten or fifteen, when the battle raged fearfully for two forenoons in succession. It seemed impossible for the little blue birds to "hold the fort;" but they did, and all was quiet for the remainder of the season. The next year the blue birds were on hand promptly, and had got nicely to work when they were attacked by an army of swallows, and in the contest, which raged fearfully for several days, were ousted, and the swallows came out masters and peacefully enjoyed the little house for the balance of the season. Last year was only a repetition of the past two years, only the blue bird had to contend with both the martins and swallows in succession. The blue birds triumphed and held the house till they had raised two families of childlren. This year, after getting fairly settled, the little blue birds have had to contend with a new enemy in the shape of a pair of robins, and they are vanquished and nowhere to be seen. The robins now hold the house and bid fair to do so until next fall.

daniel-wolfe-urbana-1881-10.A1: A man named Daniel Wolfe, who had just been released from the Illinois penitentiary after serving a sixteen years' sentence, created a terrible excitement and came near being lynched at Urbana, Illinois, a few days ago. He persuaded, by plausible tales, a young woman of good character to go with him to his home, ostensibly to remain with his family a few weeks while he was absent on a visit to Indiana. He had no home to take her to, really, but taking her with him he forced her to stay all night with him in a haystack in the country. She escaped from him the next morning, and returning to her home told her story of sorrow and distress. Immediately a crowd started in pursuit of the wretch, and after a long chase succeeded in capturing him. He was taken before a magistrate, and by that officer committed to jail, but while on the way an incensed crowd attacked him, and throwing a rope over his neck dragged him from the wagon and across the road to hang him, bruising him up very badly, but the officers cut the rope and rescued him and lodged him in jail, despite the efforts of the would-be lynchers to the contrary.

A. Oscar Jones, late Captain of the Grey Invincibles who participated in the 2nd (Gen. Harranft's) Division of the procession yesterday was a young man deserving of all commendation for his success in raising the standard of his race as militia men in his native State. After the donning of the soldier's uniform, upon the adoption of the 15th amendment there was a rapid decline, and colored soldiers became a byword of reproach; but Mr. Jones so persisted in his efforts that his company won the admiration of the entire community and the honor shown him by the State Fencibles, one of the oldest and most aristocratic militia organizations of the United States, is an evidence of the esteem in which he was held. There are not a few reminiscences of the career of Captain Alonzo Oscar Jones that are deserving of the widest publication.

The Funeral of Captain A. O. Jones of the Gray Invincibles N. G. Pa. took place on Sunday 27th inst., and it was very largely attended by the citizens of this city. The Gray Invincibles looked well. Beloved captain rest in peace!

Turner is a slender-build, copper-colored negro, and says he is nineteen years old. The last Legislature passed a law to
take the sense of the people of the State as to the necessity of calling a Convention to revise the Constitution, and accordingly the question will be voted on at the August election. Article XII of the Constitution as it stands provides that, when a majority of the members of the two Houses of the Legislature within the first twenty days of the session, concur, they may pass a law to take the sense of the people as to the necessity of calling a Convention. The question shall be submitted to the people at the next general election, and if a majority of all the voters of the State vote therefor, at the next meeting of the Legislature the question shall a second time be submitted to the people, and if a majority of the voters favor the proposition, the Legislature must call a Constitutional Convention.

This section renders it almost an impossibility to ever change the document, and its makers were thus particular with reference to a change so that no interference could be made in regard to slavery, much feared at the time. That institution having been abolished, all laws in reference to it have become dead letters, while a change in the times has rendered many other of the articles void and inoperative. That there is a necessity for a revision no thinking man will deny, and, this being the case, it becomes the people to turn out en masse and vote to call a Convention. The question has been put to the people several times, but owing to the failure of the masses to understand or to care whether a change is made or not, the necessary majority of all the voters in the State has never been obtained. We fear a like result will follow the coming effort to get a majority. The people have it in their power to vote on either side of the question, and if they fail to vote at all it is hardly fair that it should be taken that they are opposed to the change. Every effort should be made to poll as large a vote as possible, but if it is largely in favor of calling the Convention and does not reach the necessary majority, it should become the duty of the next Legislature to take revolutionary measures toward a change, by appointing the time and place for holding a Convention and asking the people to send delegates to it. The duty of such a Convention would be to make the needed changes in the Constitution, and it would then remain for the people to adopt or reject it at the polls. We wish that every voter could be made to understand the importance of his vote in the matter, and we suggest that officers of the election take special pains to ask each man to vote on the question.

It really does seem that the country is experiencing the evil effects of a moral collapse of unexampled character. Not a week, a day—nay, an hour—passes by without some revelation of a desperate crime being made. No section of the country is free from lawless deeds; no class of society is exempt from the presence of the crimson stains of violence. Thoughtful people are roused by the number and startling character of the crimes which are being committed everywhere. The germs of the epidemic seem to pervade the whole moral atmosphere; corrupting, enraging and nerving the victims of the disorder to deeds of death. The crime craze has reached the higher social circles, and all sorts of scandals and peccadillos result therefrom. Indeed, among the high and the low, the rich and the poor, the learned and the unlearned, there seems to have been a complete letting down of moral principle; and instead of peace and safety, a reign of crime has been inaugurated. The records of a single day's development of crime would fill a volume. To day, a negro in Louisiana attempts a dastardly outrage on a young lady; to morrow morning's sun will greet a ghastly corpse swinging to the limb of a tree. A jail guard in Arkansas opens the door of the prison and allows a quartette of dangerous desperadoes to go their way. In another part of the same State, a howling mob takes from the jail a prisoner under a long sentence, shoot, and then hang him. In Rutherford county, Tennessee, a negro man, for a brutal outrage, is seized by a mob of lynchers, and speedily dispatched. Two murders and one legal execution took place in Arkansas last Friday, and on the same day two men were killed in affrays, one hanged by the officers of the law in Henry county, Missouri, while at Maryville, in the same State, two youths, convicted of the crime of killing their own father, were put to death by the Sheriff in accordance with the sentence of a court. In Texas several persons were wounded and bruised in affrays, and some were killed outright on this same fatal Friday. We read of Italian bandits domiciled in New Orleans, and the next instant our eyes behold the bloody records of American brigands, who stopped a whole train, killed the conductor and a passenger, and carried away the contents of the express safe. But we have no disposition to extend the list further. It is a sickening record. The crimes include every variety and grade. Crime against life, against property, against virtue, against morality; the violent struggle of infuriated men, the stealthy shot of the concealed assassins; the pitiless embrace of the lusty brute; the invasion of the sanctities of home; slanders and lapses of every grade and character constitute a part of the records of the crimes of a week.

What can be the matter? Is the moral world out of joint? May there not be some subtle influence—some atmospheric conditions that act upon the cerebral organs to produce a species of madness? Whether that be the case or not, certain it is that the country seems to be afflicted with an epidemic of crime, such as his never before swept over it. The moral tone of the people and the press appear to be low. Mob law is justified and defended by public prints, and deeds of violence seem to excite but a passing consideration. Something must be done to check the reign of lawlessness. What is the cause? No remedy can be applied without a knowledge of the nature of the disease.

A COWARDLY CRIME.
Ten Respectable Citizens Charged With a Serious Offense.
Yesterday morning a Deputy United States Marshal arrived in the city by the train on the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, having in custody ten respectable citizens of Montgomery county, who are charged with a very serious crime. It appears that on the night of the 2d of May last a party of disguised men visited the house of a colored man by the name of Jerry Hamilton, who in some manner had rendered himself obnoxious, and taking him therefrom carried him some distance and beat him so badly that he died from the effects of the injuries then received. This outrage occurred near Mount Vernon, the county site of Montgomery, and on the following day, when the news of the outrage was circulated, a large mass meeting of the citizens was called, at which resolutions were passed condemning in the strongest terms the cowardly crime, and pledging the assistance of the authorities to ferret out the perpetrators.

In the meanwhile, information was received in Savannah, and United States Commissioner Wade issued a warrant against a number of respectable citizens, charging them with a violation of the civil rights bill in connection with this crime, and a Deputy Marshal was instructed to execute the same. The names of the gentlemen who have thus been arrested, and who, we are informed, are among the most prominent and worthy citizens of Montgomery, the very last men to countenance such an outrage, are Messrs. Joseph Palmer, William Adams, Thomas Norris, Angus Norris, Algernon Brady, R. Brady, H. Brady, W. Darley and James Buckan. There appears to be no evidence against these parties, and they were arrested merely on suspicion. The offense with which they are charged does not, we understand, come under the civil rights bill.

They were arraigned yesterday morning before the Commissioner, who issued the warrant, but, the witnesses for the prosecution not being present, they would have been committed to jail but for the interposition of their attorneys, Messrs. Garrard & Melerim, who rendered ample bond for their appearance. Mr. P. W. Carswell, of Mount Vernon, is also associated with Messrs. Garrard & Meldrim for the defense. An examination in the case will be held to day at 12 o'clock.

The Montgomery County Affair.
The citizens of Montgomery county, the particulars of whose arrest, on a warrant issued by United States Commissioner of Internal Revenue, were given in the News, were yesterday arraigned before the Commissioner in accordance with the continuance of the previous day. The witnesses for the prosecution were not present. The principal witness is a colored woman, and the affidavit upon which the warrant was issued against these gentlemen was made, we are informed, by a negro, who bears a notorious character, and whom, it is stated, would not be belived on oath by many who know him.

Messrs. Garrard & Meldrim, as counsel for the accused, in connection with Mr. P. W. Carswell, of Mt. Vernon, objected to giving bond for any further preliminary examination, and tendered bonds for their appearance to await the action of the grand jury of the United States Court, which meets in November next.

The Commissioner thereupon fixed the bonds at $2,000 for each of the accused, and the required amount was promptly furnished, some twenty-five citizens of Montgomery county sending Messrs. Garrard & Meldrim power of attorney to sign their names to any bonds that might be exacted. This shows the estimation in which the gentlemen charged with the offenses are held by their neighbors.

They have been subjected to great inconvenience and loss of time and brought a long distance, only to find that their accusers are not ready to confront them.

They left for home: yesterday afternoon by the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway train.

Desperate Duel Between Negroes.
ATLANTA, GA., August 2.—A report comes from Monroe county of a duel between two negroes, Bill Comer and Frank Cheney, at a negro wood-chopping. They quarretled, a challenge passed and was accepted, when they proceeded to settle matters on the spot in accordance with the code, the weapons being pistols. Cheney used a Derringer which missed fire. Comer, with a revolver, lodged a ball in Cheney's thigh. Again Cheney's Derringer failed, and be received another ball in the leg. Trying his Derringer once more without success, he threw it down, and seizing an axe struck at Comer, who warded off the blow and shot Cheney dead at close range. Comer escaped.

juan-monterea-taos-1881-06-11.A7: IT IS NOT prudent to advise a New Mexican rough to subject himself to the slavish customs of common decency and ordinary morality, at least so it proved the other day. An unfortunate, but apparently well-meaning man named Gallagher, at Santa Fe, undertook to remonstrate with Juan Montera for his unfilial behavior in habitually abusing his mother. The irate rowdy instantly responded by striking his admonishing friend dead with a hoe, while the moral sense of the community was vindicated immediately by lynching the disrespectful Juan. The story could not be prepared for a Sunday-school book without a little previous editing, but it serves as an incident in the current history of that stirring locality.

Tragical Tales.
Near Mt. Vernon, Ky., on the 18th inst., James Hart shot Andrew Baker dead. They were both drunk, and Hart claims that the shooting was accidental.

Johu McCombe, a prominent Colorado politician shot and probably fatally wounded James McDonald, an actor, at Leadville, Col., on the 17. Cause, misunderstanding in regard to the use of a buggy.

Robert B. Cyphert, a leading citizen of Marion county, Arkansas, was shot by an assassin while standing in his doorway.

A crazy man shot and severely wounded Miss Fannie Walker at Elizabethtown, N. J., on the 17th inst., and then killed himself.

Thos. Meyer, of Rantowles, S. C., crazed by religion, shot his 13-year-old boy as a sacrifice on the 13th. He failed in the attempt to murder two more of his children. The murderous father persuaded his little son to walk ahead of him on the road, and then deliberately shot him down.

A printers' strike at Pittsburgh, Pa., resulted in a tragedy on the 16th inst. One of the displaced men named Michael Corcoran, assaulted a "rat" and was shot dead.

At a saw-mill fifteen miles from Hot Springs, Ark., on the 15th inst., R. L. Justice was shot with a rifle by a man named Gregg, who had also recently killed a negro.

Juan Monterea, of Toas, New Mexico, killed Lem Gallagher with a hoe, for interfering in a fight with his mother. A lynching party swung Mouterea from the court house railing on the same evening.

Geo. L. Larkin, deputy United States marshal, killed his cousin, also named Larkin, at Rogerville, Tenn., on the 15th inst. The deceased had violated the laws and was resisting arrest when shot down.

Clay Wilson, a notorious gambler, was shot dead at Denver, Col., on the 16th, by James Moor, another of the gentry.

At Bedford, Ind., Wm. Brannan was shot by a concealed assassin and instantly killed.

Robert Martin shot his wife and child, a girl three years old, at Newark, N. J., on the 15th inst. The woman was instantly killed and his child mortally wounded.

Freeman Alvoirs, a lunatic, was murdered by Byron L. Day, a fellow unfortunate at Wauwatosa, Milwaukee county, Wis., on the 13th inst.

Two neck-tie sociables on the 13th inst.—one at Denver, Ark., and the other at Weston, Neb. At the former place Emory, a murderer, was taken from jail and hung; and at the latter village Charles Diddell, a negro rapist, had his neck stretched by an angry populace.

Timothy Mahoney, a policeman, was shot dead by burglars at Chicago, on the night of the 12th inst.

Wm. Gordon and Peter Magnus quarrelled at Chicago on the 12th, when Magnus kicked Gordon in the neck, causing instant death.

Patrick Mallory was shot and killed by James McDonough at Cincinnati, on the night of the 12th.

SAM S. JONES and Dell Kribs, both young men, went over the dam at Marshalltown, Iowa, and were drowned.

LUDINGTON, Mich., has been almost destroyed by fire. The entire business portion of the town is swept away. Loss about $200,000.

A PARTY of armed men took possession of the jail at Dover, Pope County, Ark., on the 13th, and hung Cal. Emery, the wife-murderer, whose death sentence Governor Churchill a few weeks since commuted to twenty-one years' imprisonment in the Penitentiary. Emery resisted and was shot in the head. It was supposed he was dead when hanged.

THE jury in the Victoria disaster investigation, at London, Out., have found a verdict censuring the owner, captain, and engineer of the ill-fated vessel. The Government Inspector is also held to blame.

OWING to violations of treaty stipulations existing between the Governments of the United States and Mexico, the Governor of Texas has issued a proclamation with a view of putting a stop to them.

MR. CLIVE HERSEE, a well-known member of the Solden Opera Company, committed suicide by jumping from a bridge into the river near Central City, Colo. His matrimonial relations were unhappy.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., has been constituted a port of delivery.

A SPECIAL from Winnepeg says war has broken out between the Sioux and Crees. A battle has been fought near the Moody Mountain, in which twenty-eight of the former were killed.

The recent fire at Quebec, according to official reports, destroyed 642 houses, rendering 1,211 families, or 6,028 people, homeless. Two-thirds of these lost their all, and had no insurance.

It is reported that DeLesseps' canal project on the Isthmus of Panama does not progress favorably. Stations have been abandoned, brigades disbanded and many engineers have returned home and workmen have been discharged. The Star and Herald says: "We would like to see a little more accomplished on the isthmus, and a little less blowing in Paris about the business."

The Illinois State Board of Health has issued a circular to the different health authorities of the Northwest inviting them to a conference at Chicago, on June 29, to take into consideration a plan for concert of action, in connection with the National Board of Health, to prevent the introduction into this country and spread of smallpox. The prevalence of small-pox at this time is noteworthy. It is now known to exist at seven points in Illinois, and is mainly owing, it is asserted, to its introduction by immigrants.

NEAR Weston, Platte County, Mo., a negro named Charles Didell assaulted a young lady named Nancy Stillwell, and after a violent struggle, in order to shield himself from the discovery of his crime, cut his victim's throat. He was discovered by two ladies passing by, who gave the alarm. The villain fled, but was pursued and captured by a party of citizens, forced to confess, and was then hanged to a bridge, the brother of the victim adjusting the noose.

SILAS M. WAITE, until recently President of the First National Bank of Brattleboro, Vt., has been found guilty of fraud and embezzlement and sentenced to six years' imprisonment in the House of Correction.

JUAN MONTEREA killed Leon M. Gallagher in Taos County, N. M., and was hanged by the vigilantes.

GEN. R. C. NEWTON, who was sent by the Governor of Arkansas to investigate the troubles in Perry County, has returned and reports everything quiet and the affair greatly exaggerated. He says the civil officers are amply able to enforce the laws, and anticipates no further disturbances.

At Rogers' Mills, Ga., the other day, Mr. and Mrs. John Middleton were drowned while boating.

ROBERT MARTIN, an Englishman, 50 years of age, living in Newark, N. J., shot his wife and child on the 14th. The woman was almost instantly killed. The child, a girl two years and six months old, was wounded in two places, it is thought fatally. Martin was arrested.

MYERS and Brown, the New Madrid (Mo.) murderers, have been sentenced to be hanged on the 15th of July, and Mitebell, as accessory to the crime, has been sentenced to thirty years' in the Penitentiary.

PATRICK Morris and Thomas Regan perished in a fire at Pierrepont's stores, Brooklyn, N. Y., on the 15th. The loss on bonded goods and buildings is estimated at $100,000.

The two stages running between Fayetteville and Alma, Ark., were both robbed on the night of the 15th, near a point where they pass each other, about twenty miles north of Alma. The north-bound stage first came along and was stopped: the robbers, two in number, presenting their revolvers at the head of the driver, compelled him to dismount and have his hands secured, after doing which they blindfolded and bound the passengers, at the same time relieving them of their valuables. The other stage soon put in an appearance and the driver and passengers were put through a similar programme. The robbers did not get a very heavy return for their labors, only about $35 in cash and a gold watch and chain.

SHOT AND KILLED WRILE PLOUGHING.
VINCENNES, Ind., Aug. 15.—In the White River bottoms, twenty miles southeast of Vincennes, Lake Mosby, from the ambush of a hedge, fired two rifle balls into the body of Lawson Hewett while the latter was ploughing in his field last Friday afternoon. Hewett was killed. The men had each lost corn cribs by fire and had each accused the other of incendiarism.

FATAL DUEL IN THE INDIAN NATION.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Aug. 15.—A desperate duel was fought last week in the Indian Nation between T. O. Carpenter, a Choctaw chief, and Colonel Amos Price, a prominent citizen of the Creek Nation. Price was killed and Carpenter was fatally wounded. Considerable feeling exists over the affair, as both men were among the most prominent in the Nation.

MURDERED IN A QUARREL.
St. Louis, Aug. 15.—At a low den on the island in the Mississippi River opposite Hannibal, about 3 o'clock yesterday morning, Winston Barnes and John Gibbons got into a quarrel. Barnes shot Gibbons through the body and Boyd Robinson plunged a knife into his neck, severing the jugular vein. Gibbons fell to the floor and expired almost instantly. The parents of Gibbons live at Dubuque, Iowa.

KILLING HIS MOTHER'S LOVER.
DETROIT, Aug. 15.—John Allguire, age twenty-three years, surrendered himself to the Sheriff at Grand Haven, this State, last night, stating that he had just shot and killed Frederick Green, colored, who for several years had lived at Grand Haven with Allguire's mother. Allguire said that Green got into a quarrel with his mother, and struck her on the head with a gun, and also attacked him. He shot Green in self-defence. The top of Green's head was blown off. In the fight between Green and his mistress the latter's skull was fractured by the blow given her by Green.

ATTEMPTED JAIL-ESCAPE. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
KANSAS CITY, Aug. 15. Bill Ryan, one of the noted gang of thieves who robbed the Chicago & Alton train at Glendale, Mo., in November, 1870, with the James boys, made a bold attempt to escape from the County Jail in this city to-day. Ryan was brought to Kansas City from Tennessee about a month ago, and is known to have been one of the Glendale gang. The officers have suspected that something was wrong for more than two weeks, but could find nothing tangible upon which to base their suspicions, except the unusual noise that was kept up in the jail at all hours, and the regularity with which Ryan appeared at his cell-door with a newspapor held up in front of him whenever any one came by. This morning Marshal Murphy determined to make an examination of his cell. They found a bunch of five steel burglars' saws, and the evidence of their use in the iron floor. He had cut three sides of a square about two foot wide, and was within four inches of completing the fourth. The floor cut through, it would have been the work of but a few hours to reinvoe the back floor, tunnel under the oge, come up in the corridor, and escape through one of the windows. Ryan tried to lay the blame on his collimate, but, falling, said the saws wore there when he came to the cell, which is known to be a lie.

STOLE COUNTERFEIT MONEY,
LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Aug. 15.—Ned Lawson, janitor at the United States Court-room, was arrested to-day on a charge of stealing counterfeit money from the office of the Prosecuting Attorney and attempting to pass the same. He was taken before United States Commissioner Hompstead for examination, but asked and had the case continued till next Monday. The evidence against him is conclusive. Lawson is one of the most prominent colored men in the State, being a member of the colored Masons, Odd-Follows, Knights Templar, and Wise Men. He has been janitor at the court-room for five years.

THE GRAND HAVEN TRAGEDY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
GRAND HAVEN, Mich., Aug. 15.—Evidence before the Coronor's inquest over the bodies of Loveloss Green and Mrs. Alguire, murdered last evening, is all in, but the verdict is not rendered. But little doubt exists that their verdict will be that Alguire killed both his mother and the negro. The evidence against him is entirely circumstantial. He says Green shot his mother before he shot Green, but no bullet-wounds are on her body. He threatened to kill both.

STARBING AFFRAY. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 16. — Peter Hughes, one of the men stabbed into last night by William Bailey, alias "Dago Bill," died at the Sisters' Hospital at 9 o'clock this afternoon. Bailey was met by Hughes and a young man named Baughman in the Marble Hall saloon, and the two began "skylarking" with him. At last the fun was carried too far, and when Hughes threw his arms about Bailey's neck, and Baughman had his hand in his pocket, he struck at them with a knife, cutting both. Baughman only received a slight cut in the chest, but his companion received a terrible stab in the abdomen, from which he never rallied. SAFE ACROSS THE BORDER.
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo., Aug. 10.—Mr. Willis, the Warden of the Missouri Penitentiary, received a telegram to-day from his son, who went as State Agent to Halifax to bring back the notorious swindler and bogus priest Gallen Derohan, with a score of alluses, who escaped from the Missouri Penitentiary some months ago, stating that the authorities there refused to give him up on the ground that forgery, the crime of which he was convicted. is not an offense for which a prisoner is subject to extradition. It is stated in this connection by Mr. Willis that the document to which President Garfield attached his signature a few days ago was the extradition paper in this case.

TRAIN-WRECKERS.

GALVESTON, Tex., Aug. 10.—A San Antonio special says an unsuccessful attempt was made yesterday to wreck an excursion-train having on board 550 men, women, and children, by laying ties across the track. The train was going at the rate of thirty miles an hour when the engine struck the ties, which were thrown from the track, badly bruising five men riding on the cow-catcher.

THE GRAND HAVEN MURDER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
GRAND HAVEN, Mich., Aug. 10.—The Coroner's jury rendered a verdict this morning that John Alguiro killed both his mother and the colored man Green,—the negro by shooting him in the head with the shotgun, and his mother by a blow on the back of the head with the stock of the gun, which was broken.

ASSASINATED. Memphis, Tenn., Aug. 10.—Henry Foster, a colored farmer, five miles north of Covington, Tenn., was called out of his house last night and shot to death. The assasin escaped.

HYMENEAL.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune,
BLOOMINGTON, Ill., Aug. 16.—Mr. Edward B. Gridley and Miss Ora Wulton, two leading members of Bloomington society, were united in marriage at noon to-day at the home of the bride on East Locust street in the presence of a few intimate friends and relatives. As Mr. Gridley is perhaps the wealthiest young man in McLean County, and both groom and bride are greatly respected, the event was one of far more than ordinary importance. The Rev. Dr. Read, pastor of the First Baptist Church, spoke the mystic words, and after handshaking and farewells the happy pair took the Chicago & Alton train for Chicago and the East. They will be absent about three weeks, visiting Coney Island, Isle of Shoals, and other watering-places, and on their return will take up permanently their residence here, for the time occupying part of the magnificent Gridley homestead. Mr. Gridley is the younger son of Gen. Ashbel Gridley, whose recent death was chronicled by Dirk Turrone, and who was one of the ablest financiers and lawyers and most public spirited men who have ever lived in Central Illinois. His bride is the eldest daughter of John T. Walton, plow manufacturer, an old an honored citizen and prominent business man. She is a graceful and stately brunette and has been much admired and honored by Bloomington society, of which she has always been a leading mem-

ber. She was dressed in a travelling costume of surah satin of hunter's green, trimmed in green and gold, with bonnet to match, face at throat fastened with a costly and beautiful brooch of diamonds presented by the groom. The groom wore a plain and simple business suit. The wedding was entirely devoid of show and ostentation.

CASUALTIES.

ACCIDENT AT A COAL-SHAFT.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
CENTRALIA, Ill., Aug. 16.—Last night William Craig, out of curiosity, went behind the wires stretched to guard the coal-shaft, and craned his neck over the hole just in time to catch the cage. It started ten feet above and came down with a rush, jamming Craig's head between it and the curbing, and crushing that member to an unrecognizable mass. Marks of the teeth were left in the hard wood of the curbing. Craig was a well-known and respected man and leaves many relatives here. He was not married.

NEWS OF THE WEEK.

MICHIGAN.

John Aulguive a Frenchman shot and killed his mother's paramour, a colored man named Lovels Green with whom she had been living at Grand Haven. Aulguive claims that Green shot his mother who was found dead in the same room and that he killed Green in revenge. It is believed that young Aulguive quarrelled with and killed both.

Otto Lang while prowling around the yard of Bowman Van Kuren at Greenville was shot by VanKuren, 70 shots taking effect in his neck causing a dangerous wound. There's a woman in the case as usual.

Mrs. Erastus Yeomana, 74 years old and an early settler of Ionia, was found dead in her room.

Voscamp, the man who murdered Lyman Cady, near Coopersville, some months ago, and who narrowly escaped lynching by an infuriated gang of Cady's neighbors, has been taken to Grand Rapids for safe-keeping.

Base Ball—Cleveland 8, Detroit 5.

Mrs. Cotton, living near the city limits of Detroit, heard a noise in her cellar, and discovering two men there, shot one of them, then looked them in and went for the police. The burglars succeeded in making their escape during her absence, but were traced some distance by a trail of blood.

Chas. Hubbard of Fenton, has lost a barn by fire, the second one within a year.

Thomas Cooper, aged 81, fell dead in the office of a Paw Paw lawyer, while he was transacting some business.

Mahon Barnbart of Union township, aged 60, a prominent citizen of Branch Co., dropped dead at his residence.

R. Kibble, a well-to-do farmer of the township of Browne, has been arrested on complaint of Rhoda Hoyt, a young woman who charges that Kibble is the father of her illegitimate child. Kibble is a married man.

Melissa Yeck, age 15, was killed at Dimondale while riding, by the horse being frightened and hacking the buggy over an embankment.

James Riley and William Burns broke out of jail at Cheboygan. They were charged with larceny. A reward of $100 is offered for their apprehension.

State Board of Equalization met at Lansing 16th. Lieut. Gov. Crosby was chosen chairman.

The Agricultural College commencement exercises took place at Lansing on the 16th.

Two former residents of Fenton have recently shipped over 1,000 sheep from Michigan to their farms in Kansas.

The coroner's jury at Grand Haven rendered a verdict that John Alguire killed both his mother and the colored man Green; the latter by shooting him in the head with the shot gun and his mother by a blow on the back of the head with the stock of the gun, which was broken.

Base Ball, Cleveland 6, Detroit 5.

Prof. E. W. Wetmore of the Detroit high school resigns to accept the superintendency of the Detroit lined oil work.

Four men entered a flouring mill at Mt. Clemens and while one engaged the attention of the proprietor the others secured $40 from the money drawer. They were discovered and captured. The same morning Mrs. Bush of Louisville Ky., a boarder of the Avery House, lost $1,200 worth of jewelry from her room. She heard and saw a party in the room but supposed it to be a lady friend who occupied an adjoining room. No clue yet to the thief.

A man fell down a well 80ft. deep at Grand Haven. The doctors are reported still in attendance.

Mrs. Miranda Smith, wife of Moses R. Smith, died at her home in Ada, Kent county, Michigan. Mrs. Smith lived in St. Clair county for many years. Her home will be remembered by many of the lumbermen and raftmen, located a few miles from Port Huron on the banks of Black River. They made her house their home during the many years that lumbering and rafting was carried on in this section.

A large portion of the village of Alleytown was burned on the 17th.

The "Matrimonial Aid Society of Michigan has been organized in Detroit.

Mayor Stekette of Grand Rapids had a saloon keeper named Creme arrested for disorderly conduct. Creme was fined $50. Later Creme had the Mayor arrested for false imprisonment and a local justice has fined the Mayor $50 on this charge. Appealed.

The state board of agriculture have accepted the resignation of Fox, the steward of the college.

The reunion of the Lapeer county soldiers' and sailors' association at Hadley was a great success. About 4,000 persons were present. An elegant picnic dinner was furnished all, and addresses were made by Gov. Jerome, Congressman Rich, Adjutant-general Robertson and others.

Base Ball: Detroit 3, Cleveland 0.

Eighty of the Allegan County pioneers have been pioneering at Allegan.

The Alleytown fire burned 35 buildings. Twenty families are houseless. The loss is estimated at $60,000.

The spoke factory of F. H. Starkey at Howard City, have been burned. Loss, $3,000, uninsured.

Con. B. Mallory of the Lansing House succeeds Fox as steward of the State Agricultural College.

David Marshall an escaped convict from the Jackson State prison has been captured and returned to that institution.

Frank Moore of Mt. Clemens went out crow hunting early and when he returned, his wife, who had just finished breakfast, was kneeling down to say her morning prayers. He was dragging the loaded gun behind him, when the door swung shut, striking the hammer of the gun and discharging the piece, the whole load taking effect in one of Mrs. Moore's legs. The wound was a very painful one, but not necessarily serious.

Gen. N. Church, Quartermaster of the State Commissioners, has concluded arrangements with the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Company, to carry the Governor and staff, Legislature and State troops over the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad to Washington for the Yorktown celebration, leaving Jackson and Detroit October 15, reaching Washington Sunday afternoon, remaining in Washington until Monday evening, then taking a steamer for Yorktown, returning from Yorktown Friday evening for Washington.

Detroit exported only $2,496 in breadstuffs during July. Same month last year $110,-698.

Rase Ball—Akron 8; Detroit 6.

E. B. Ives was elected vice-president for Michigan of the photographers convention at New York.

James Curley had his head mashed and was instantly killed by being struck by the hammer of a pile driver at Belle Isle.

Sophie Lyons has secured ball at Jackson.

Dr. MacVicar, of the state normal school, has resigned to take a place in the baptist theological seminary at Toronto, Ont.

Frank Montgomery, 18 years old, was killed on W. S. Gerrish's logging railroad in Clare county.

CONCERTED MURDER.

A WIFE-MURDERER.

CINCINNATI, O., April 22.—Shortly before midnight to night, John Mooney was arrested for the murder of his wife. The crime was not known to the police nor the public, though the act was committed last Sunday, because her death did not occur until this evening. The Coroner being called in, discovered that the woman died from the effects of a wound inflicted by a batchet. It appears that Mooney has always been passionate and abusive, especially when drunk. Defendants' Counsel Move For a New Hearing,

An Appeal Taken to the Supreme Court.
The Prisoners Carried to Nashville.
with the following jurors, who were selected from a panel of over 200 men:
Noah Smith, A. J. Sutherland, Abraham Brazelton, W. M. Hall, John Schnell, J. L. W. Bennett, Wm. Purdam, J. L. Brandon, Wm. Stevens, Wm. Lynch, H. H. Holt, and S. C. M. Williams. Constable Alex. Caldwell, officer in charge.
A large number of witnesses—about 40, including both sides—were examined, which occupied the time of the Court until 5 o'clock Thursday evening, the 14th, and in two hours afterward (7 o'clock) the argument was opened by the Attorney-General with a two hours' speech. He was followed by Messrs. W. E. Colyar and P. R. Curtis, counsel for the defendants.
Friday morning Capt. T. D. Gregory spoke in behalf of the State, closing just before noon, and the afternoon was consumed by Messrs. John Simmons and Jesse Arledge, defendants' counsel.

Gov. Marks, for the State, made the closing argument. He commenced at 7 o'clock Friday night, and spoke till 9:30, when Judge Williams charged the jury, and the Court adjourned till next morning.

Saturday morning the jury appeared and requested that Judge Williams give further explanation in regard to the charge. The Judge said the only explanation he could make would be to re-read the charge, which he did in his usual articulate style, when the jury retired to their room in the Ballard House. This was about 10 o'clock.

At 1:30 p. m. the jury returned to the Court-room and rendered a verdict: Guilty of murder in the first degree. The counsel for defendants moved for a new hearing, and Court adjourned till Monday morning.

At 9 o'clock Monday morning Court was called. The movement of defendants' counsel for a new hearing was over-ruled. Judge W. then remarked that he was about to perform one of the most solemn duties of his life, and asked the prisoners if they had anything to say before sentence was passed upon them. John Poe raised to his feet and said that they had not been given a fair trial, that prejudice was high against them, that evidence had been produced which was untrue, that he could have produced witnesses whose testimony would have been valuable to them if he had been given time, &c. He then took his seat, and the death sentence was pronounced. Judge Williams said:

"It is the judgment of the Court that you, John Poe and Cicero Poe, be delivered to the Sheriff of Franklin county, to be put and kept in the jail of said county until Friday, the 17th day of June, 1881, and from thence taken by said Sheriff to a gallows within one mile of the Courthouse of Winchester, there to be hanged, each and severally, until you are dead. Said Sheriff shall erect said gallows and said defendants shall pay the costs of this prosecution."

After the sentence was passed, John Poe said, very audibly: "I guess I won't be at that scaffold."

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, and at 11:30 o'clock Sheriff Turner, with a sufficient guard, left for Nashville with the prisoners, where they will remain until their case is acted upon by the Supreme Court, which meets next December. If the lower Court has erred in the trial they will get a new hearing; if to the contrary, the death sentence will be confirmed and another day be set by that body for their execution.

The Court adjourned about 11 o'clock, and Judge Williams left for Spencer to hold Court for the balance of the week. He will return and hold a special term here next week, commencing on Monday, for the purpose of trying those cases on the felony docket which were not continued.

We do not give the testimony of the witnesses in this trial, because we did not hear it all, other and more important business requiring our attention. It is enough to say, however, that, so far as our knowledge goes, the prisoners were given a fair and impartial trial, and the testimony produced against them corroborated what we printed at the time of their arrest; and, furthermore, the verdict accords, almost universally, with the views of the hundreds of persons who were present during the trial.

Murder in a Dance-House.
EX DREW  THE COLORED PROBLEM
Murder in a Dance-House.

POSEY DREW, THE COLORED PROPRIETOR, STABBED TO DEATH FOR REFUSING ADMITTANCE TO A MINOR—ARREST OF THE ALLEGED CRIMINAL—INQUEST TO BE HELD TO-DAY, &C.

Last night about 8 o'clock a difficulty occurred in a negro dance-house at 1807 east Carv street (better known as "Cash Corner"), which resulted in the death by stabbing of Posey Drew (colored), the proprietor of the house. The particulars of the affair, as far as could be ascertained, are as follows: About the hour above named a party consisting of one man and three boys or youths went to the house for the purpose, it is supposed, of attending a dance which was to take place there. Drew objected to one of the boys going in because he was too young, when a controversy ensued between him and the visitors, during which Fannie Chalkley, a mulatto woman who was present, shoved two of the boys out of the door, leaving Drew and the man and the oldest of the youths together. The woman states that she saw the youth hand his companion a knife, and in a few moments heard Drew exclaim "I'm cut to death! Run for the police." The party then ran off. She immediately ran out into the street and commenced to cry "murder," and when she returned she found Drew lying on the floor weltering in blood, and in a few moments he expired.

News of the difficulty was conveyed to the First police-station and Sergeant Howard and Officer Walton went to the spot. At the same time Captain Pleasants telegraphed to Dr. Brock. When the officers arrived it was found that the man was dead, and the Coroner was notified.

From a description given of the parties suspicion was attracted to a man by the name of Charles Bowen as the party who did the cutting, and William Gilham, a youth of about eighteen years, as one of the parties who were present. Githam was found at the Theatre Comique by Sergeant Howard and Officer Walton, and when brought to the station-house was identified by the woman Fannie Chalkley as one of the party whom she shoved out of the door. Bowen subsequently came to the station-house and delivered himself up. He admitted being present during the cutting, but denies that he was one of the party, and says that the fatal blow was struck over his shoulder, but does not know who did it. Bowen bears rather a bad reputation, having served a term in the penitentiary, and also in the chain-gang.

The murdered man was about forty years of age, and, strange as it may seem, was looked upon as a quiet and well-behaved person, notwithstanding the fact that he kept a house that was resorted to by the most degraded of both sexes and color.

Drs. Brock and Taylor made a partial examination of the wound, which had the appearance of being made with a large knife, and found that it had penetrated the cavity of the chest, and that death was caused from internal hemorrhage overwhelming the lungs.

Dr. Taylor will make a post mortem examination of the body this morning at 10 o'clock, and an inquest at 4 P. M.

be the absorbing topic of conversation Sunday and yesterday in the neighborhood of the occurrence, especially among the colored people, with whom the deceased was quite popular, notwithstanding the questionable character of his vocation. After our report closed Saturday night the police were scouring the city in search of persons suspected of being implicated in the crime, and several arrests were made, but, with the exception of Gilliam and Charles Bowen, who were held to await the action of the coroner's jury, in each case the parties satisfied the authorities that they had no connection with the affair, and were released. Considerable interest in the matter was also manifested in Manchester when it became known Sunday that all of the parties suspected of the crime resided in that city.

Coroner Taylor made a post-mortem examination of the remains Sunday morning at 10 o'clock, and ascertained that the wound penetrated the upper part of the right lung about 1½ inches, causing hemorrhage, which produced death in a few minutes. About 4 o'clock in the afternoon the jury, which had been previously gotten together by Deputy High-Constable Whitehead, met at the scene of the murder, and after being sworn in adjourned to the Old-Market Hall to hear the testimony in the case.

Charles Bowen (white) was the first witness examined. The Coroner told him that in view of his connection with this case that he was at liberty to decline answering any question which he thought would criminate him. Bowen stated that he lived on the Midlothian road, just outside the corporate limits of Manchester; that he went to Drew's house Saturday night about 8:15 o'clock in company with his brother John Bowen, Jim Butler, George Binn, and Michael Binn (all white); that he and two of the boys went in the house, leaving two outside. He declined to tell the names of the two who went in with him. Two of the party who went in the house had some words with Drew, who told them they must pay ten cents or go out. They went out, followed by Drew. At the door they met a colored man, and some of the party knocked up against him, or hit him, when Drew shoved the man in the house and closed the door after him, remaining outside with Bowen's party. One of the three who had gone inside handed a pocket-knife to one of the others, with which he stabbed Drew in the breast. Drew had not done anything to provoke a difficulty. Didn't think the stabbing would have been done but for the colored man coming in. Jim Butler had gone off nearly to Seventeenth street when the stabbing was done. He (Bowen) stayed about ten or twenty minutes after the stabbing, the others ran off immediately. Willie Gilliam was not there. Bowen described the person who did the stabbing as a tolerably stout fellow about sixteen years old and black hair, he thought, and left-handed. Did not think his brother was left-handed. Had been told by one of the party what became of the knife, but declined to tell. Saw only one of the boys after the difficulty. The knife was borrowed from Pat. Moore, who lives in Manchester. None of the party were any kin to him except John Bowen, his brother.

Henry Temple (colored) was the next witness. He was inside the house, with the door shut, when the stabbing occurred. Saw some of the parties as they went off, but would not be able to recognize them. He could only tell what happened after the stabbing, which did not differ materially from what we have already published.

Waddy T. Dickinson (white) knew nothing of the cutting; only knew what occurred afterwards.

Fanny Chalkley (colored) testified next. Her statement did not differ very much from that published in the Dispatch of Sunday, except she stated that when the door was opened after the cutting she saw Charles Bowen standing on the sidewalk with his hand raised and a knife in it, as if he intended to strike again. She knew Bowen, and was positive that he had the knife.

Frances Alien (colored) testified, but there was nothing new in her testimony.

Lizzie Kelly (colored) did not know what happened in the house. She was leaning out of her window (which adjoins Drew's house) at the time, and saw Drew come to the door. He stood in the door and told Frances to go and tell Beau Temple to come there. She came back and said she could not find him. He said as soon as he could get some one to attend to his business he would have that fuss stopped. He would get protection. The gentleman standing on the sidewalk said: "We got your protection here; we got your age." About that time Temple came up and started in the door, and whether he struck up against the boy or the boy struck him I don't know; but one of the boys asked him what he was doing. He told him (the boy) to get out of his way and let him get in. Posey told Temple not to have anything to say to the young men; that he could settle it; and Temple went in and Drew pulled the door to with his left hand. After he pulled the door to, one of the boys, who had on a slouched hat, handed Bowen something which looked like a knife, when he (Bowen) raised his right hand and made a motion, and Posey put both hands to his breast, and, staggering up against the door, said, "Halloo murder; I am stabbed to death. Don't let that man get away." Fanny Coleman, who lives in the house with him, ran out, and she and I got there about the same time, and Fanny put her arms around him, Drew crying out, "Hold me up; go for the doctor." She carried him in the house, and got as far as this, when she noticed the blood on him, and asked him who cut him. He then fell to the floor, and she upon him. He lived about ten minutes. When I went to the door Bowen was walking slowly up the street; the other man was on the other side of the street, near Smith's junk-store. The boys I did not see after I came out of my door. Mr. Dickinson was not in the house at that time. Drew was never put into a chair. Charles Bowen was the man who raised his hand with something shining in it. He was dressed in light clothes. I have known Bowen since 1878. I became acquainted with him in the city jail when Captain Tyler was in charge. Drew hallooed "Murder! Go for the doctor," before he was carried into the house.

This concluded all the testimony which the Coroner had been able to get up to that time, and he suggested that the jury adjourn until 4 o'clock yesterday evening, by which time he thought he would be able to get the rest of Bowen's companions, and probably other evidence which would enable the jury to determine who was the guilty party. They were then dismissed until the hour above named.

The Coroner's jury reassembled at 4 o'clock P. M. yesterday. James Butler, George Binn, and Michael Binn, three of the boys who were with Charles Bowen at Drew's on the night of the stabbing, having
